info.title: Salix API
info.description:
Salix scores recorded B2B sales calls, writes a coaching plan for the weakest skills, and lets a salesperson practise against a buyer built from the deals they lost.

Sign in with `POST /api/auth/login` or the Google flow to receive a session cookie. A deployment may also require a shared key in the `X-API-Key` header.

get.description:
Liveness plus enough state for the UI to explain itself.

The frontend shows a mode badge -- live or offline -- because a judge
should never have to wonder whether they are looking at real inference.

429.description: Too many requests. Wait for the time in the `Retry-After` header.

get.description:
Can this process actually serve a request right now?

Distinct from /health on purpose. Health says the process is alive, which
a deployment platform uses to decide whether to restart it; readiness says
the database answers, which is what decides whether to send traffic. A
process whose database has gone away is alive and must not be given work.

Deliberately cheap: one round trip, no inference, no counting. A readiness
probe that costs anything gets run every few seconds forever.

Stream the buyer's reply, then the coach nudges and updated session.

The response is a single SSE stream carrying three event types so the
client makes one request per turn: `delta` while the buyer speaks, then
`nudge`s, then the authoritative `session` state.

get.description:
Free neural speech, in a woman's voice.

Separate from /speak, which renders the buyer through Qwen TTS and needs a
key. This one needs nothing, and it is the only path here that can say an
Urdu sentence at all -- no Qwen TTS model supports Urdu, and Windows ships
no Urdu voice unless somebody installs the language pack.

A GET with the text in the query string, because the browser plays it by
handing the URL to an <audio> element, and an <audio> element cannot POST.

`lang` is the caller's own tag -- the one it hands to speech recognition --
and the provider maps it to a voice. Passing `en-PK` for Roman Urdu used to
fall through to the English voice, so the reply came back British.
